periods.name: Through the Sea into the Wilderness

events.title: Slavery in Egypt
events.subtitle: A king who did not know Joseph, and sons thrown into the river
story: In Goshen, the rich land where the Nile spills into the sea, the whole household of Jacob numbered seventy. Joseph died, and his brothers, and all that generation, yet the children of Israel had children and more children until they filled the land. Then a new king came to rule over Egypt, a king who did not know Joseph. He said to his people, look, this people is more numerous and stronger than we are. If war comes, they may join our enemies and fight against us.

Under the burning sun the sound of mud being trodden and bricks being shaped never stopped. The taskmasters drove them without rest. And so Pharaoh's store cities rose, Pithom and Rameses. Yet the harder they were oppressed, the more Israel grew and spread. The Egyptians came to dread them, and worked them more cruelly still.

Pharaoh summoned the Hebrew midwives, Shiphrah and Puah, and gave them an order. When you deliver a child, if it is a boy, kill him, and if it is a girl, let her live. But the midwives feared God, and they let the babies live. At last the king gave an order to all his people. Every boy born to the Hebrews, throw him into the Nile. From that day the waters of the Nile ran dark.

words.text: Look, the people of Israel have grown more numerous and stronger than we are. If war breaks out they may join our enemies and fight against us. Let us deal with them shrewdly.
Hebrew women are not like Egyptian women. They are strong, and they give birth before the midwife even arrives.
Every boy born to the Hebrews, throw into the Nile. You may let the girls live.

events.note: Pithom and Rameses were store cities where grain and supplies were kept. Because of the name Rameses, some date the exodus to the thirteenth century BC under Ramesses II, but this journey follows the earlier date given in 1 Kings 6:1.
events.reflect: If Scripture keeps the names of two midwives instead of the king's, whose eyes do I fear when I make my choices where no one is watching?

quiz.q: What were the names of the midwives who defied Pharaoh and saved the Hebrew babies?
quiz.explain: The midwives Shiphrah and Puah feared God; they did not do as the king commanded but let the boys live (Ex 1:15–17). God gave them families of their own (Ex 1:21).

events.title: A Basket on the Nile
events.subtitle: A baby drawn out of the river
story: A man from the house of Levi married a Levite woman, and she bore a son. Seeing what a beautiful child he was, his mother hid him for three months. But as his cries grew louder, she could hide him no longer. She wove a little basket from papyrus stalks and coated it with tar and pitch.

On the bank of the Nile, where sunlight broke on the water, the mother laid the baby in the basket and set it gently among the reeds. Then she turned away, looking back again and again, her feet unwilling to leave. While the reeds whispered in the wind, the baby's sister stood at a distance, holding her breath to see what would become of him.

Just then Pharaoh's daughter came down to the river to bathe. She saw the basket among the reeds and sent her maid to fetch it. When she opened the lid, the baby was crying. Her heart went out to him. This is one of the Hebrew children, she said. The sister stepped forward and asked whether she should go and call a nurse from among the Hebrew women, and the princess told her to go. The sister brought the baby's own mother. So the baby went back to his own mother's arms, and there he was nursed and grew. When the child was older, the princess took him as her son and named him Moses, saying, I drew him out of the water.

words.text: This must be one of the Hebrew babies.
Shall I go and find one of the Hebrew women to nurse the baby for you?
I drew him out of the water, so his name will be Moses.

events.note: The name Moses sounds like the Hebrew word masha, to draw out. Others think it comes from an Egyptian word meaning son or born of, as in the name Thutmose. The names of his parents, Amram and Jochebed, appear in Exodus 6:20.
events.reflect: If the very river that carried the order of death became the way a baby was rescued, do I believe God can work even in the place I fear most?

quiz.q: How long did Moses' mother hide him before putting him in the basket?
quiz.explain: Seeing that he was a fine child, his mother hid him for three months, and when she could hide him no longer she made the papyrus basket (Ex 2:2–3).

img.credit: James Tissot, Moses Laid Amid the Flags, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: Flight to Midian
events.subtitle: A prince sheds his robes and becomes a stranger
story: Moses, raised in the palace, grew to be a man and went out to see his own people at their hard labour. There he saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew. Moses looked this way and that, and seeing no one, he struck the Egyptian dead and buried him in the sand. He thought no one had seen.

The next day he went out again and found two Hebrews fighting. When Moses asked the one in the wrong why he was striking his fellow Hebrew, the man shot back. Who made you our ruler? Do you mean to kill me the way you killed the Egyptian? Moses was afraid. The story reached Pharaoh himself, and the king sought to kill him. Moses left everything behind and fled from Pharaoh to the land of Midian.

At a well in Midian, the seven daughters of the local priest came to water their father's flock. Shepherds came and drove them off, but Moses stood up, came to their aid and watered the flock. Their father Reuel invited him into his home. Moses stayed in that house, married Zipporah, and had a son he named Gershom. Years passed, and the king of Egypt died. The cry of Israel, groaning under slavery, rose up to God, and God heard it.

words.text: Who made you our ruler and judge? Are you planning to kill me the way you killed that Egyptian yesterday?
Where is he now? Why did you leave the man behind? Go and invite him to eat with us.
I have become a stranger in a foreign land.

events.note: Midian is thought to have been the land of nomadic peoples east of the Gulf of Aqaba, in the northwest of the Arabian Peninsula. In chapter 3 Reuel is called Jethro. Stephen says Moses was forty years old when he went to visit his own people.
events.reflect: If it was not forty years in the palace but forty years in the wilderness that shaped Moses, am I treating the hidden years after my failure as nothing but wasted time?

quiz.q: What was the name of the first son born to Moses in Midian?
quiz.explain: Moses named his son Gershom, saying, I have become a stranger in a foreign land (Ex 2:22). Eliezer is the second son, mentioned later in Exodus 18:4.

events.title: The Burning Bush
events.subtitle: A fire that burned but did not consume
story: Moses drove the flock of his father-in-law Jethro far to the other side of the wilderness. And so he came to Horeb, the mountain of God. On a silent slope of nothing but rock and dry scrub, a single bush was wrapped in flames. Yet however long he looked, the bush did not burn away. Moses stopped where he was. I must go closer and see how this can be.

As he came near, a voice called from the heart of the fire. Moses, Moses. Moses answered. Here I am. The Lord said, come no closer. Take off your sandals, for the place where you stand is holy ground. Moses took off his sandals and covered his face. He was afraid to look at God. The Lord said, I have seen the misery of my people in Egypt, and I have heard them crying out because of their taskmasters. Now I have come down to rescue them.

The Lord went on. Now go. I am sending you to Pharaoh. Moses replied. Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh? Moses held back again and again. If the people ask me your name, Lord, what shall I tell them? The Lord told him his name. I am who I am. Moses spoke again. What if they do not believe me? The Lord showed him signs. The staff he threw on the ground became a snake and writhed, and the hand he put inside his cloak came out white as snow. Still Moses pleaded once more. Lord, I am no speaker. To the man who resisted to the very end, the Lord gave his brother Aaron, saying, I will be with your mouth and with his.

words.text: I am who I am. Tell the people of Israel this: I Am has sent me to you.
I have clearly seen the suffering of my people in Egypt, and I have heard them cry out. I know their pain. Now I have come down to rescue them.
Who gave people their mouths? Is it not I, the Lord? Now go. When you speak, I will be with your mouth.
Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the people of Israel out of Egypt?

events.note: Horeb is taken to be another name for Mount Sinai. Tradition places it at Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai Peninsula, where Saint Catherine's Monastery stands at its foot, but other views place it in the northern Sinai or in the land of Midian in northwestern Arabia.
events.reflect: When Moses asked who he was to go, God answered not with his qualifications but with the promise “I will be with you”; am I still searching for that answer inside myself?

quiz.q: Before the burning bush, what did God first tell Moses to take off?
quiz.explain: God said, Do not come any closer. Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground (Ex 3:5).

img.credit: Domenichino, Landscape with Moses and the Burning Bush, c. 1610–1616 · The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Public domain

events.title: Before Pharaoh
events.subtitle: Make bricks without straw
story: Moses and Aaron entered Pharaoh's palace. Aaron spoke. Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel. Let my people go, so that they may hold a festival for me in the wilderness. The king laughed coldly. Who is the Lord, that I should obey him? I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go. That same day Pharaoh gave the taskmasters a new order.

From now on, do not give them straw for the bricks. Let them go and gather it themselves. But hold them to the same number of bricks as before. They are lazy, and that is why they clamour to go and offer sacrifices. The people scattered across the whole land of Egypt to gather stubble in place of straw. The taskmasters drove them day after day, and the Israelite foremen were beaten when the quota went unmet.

The foremen came out from their beating and stood in the way of Moses and Aaron. You have put a sword in Pharaoh's hand to kill us. Heartbroken, Moses went back to the Lord. Lord, why have you brought trouble on this people? Ever since I spoke to Pharaoh in your name, he has only grown harsher. The Lord promised again. I am the Lord. I will bring you out from under your heavy burdens and take you as my own people. Moses told them this, but broken in spirit by their cruel slavery, the people could not listen.

words.text: I am the Lord. I will bring you out from under the heavy burdens of Egypt and rescue you with an outstretched arm. I will take you as my people, and I will be your God.
Now you will see what I do to Pharaoh. Pressed by a mighty hand, he will let the people go.
Who is the Lord, that I should obey him and let Israel go? I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go.

events.note: Egyptian bricks were made by mixing straw into Nile mud and drying it in the sun. The straw held the bricks together so they would not crack. A wall painting in the tomb of Rekhmire at Thebes shows foreign labourers shaping bricks.
events.reflect: When obedience brought back only a heavier burden, Moses demanded to know why; can I accept even such an honest prayer as part of faith?

quiz.q: What did Pharaoh say he would no longer give the Israelites?
quiz.explain: Pharaoh said, Do not give them straw for the bricks as before; let them gather it themselves, and he did not let them reduce the number of bricks (Ex 5:7–8).

img.title: Moses Speaks to Pharaoh
img.credit: James Tissot, Moses Speaks to Pharaoh, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: The Ten Plagues
events.subtitle: Ten signs upon a hardened heart
story: Moses raised his staff and struck the Nile, and the river turned to blood. Dead fish floated to the surface, and the stench was so great that the Egyptians could not drink from the river. Seven days later frogs crawled up out of the river and covered everything, even the bedrooms of the palace, the ovens and the kneading bowls. The dust of the ground became gnats swarming over people and animals. Here the magicians, who had copied the signs, gave up and said to Pharaoh, this is the finger of God.

Next came swarms of flies, filling the palace and every house. But in the land of Goshen, where the Israelites lived, there was not a single one. The livestock sickened and fell, and boils broke out on people and animals. Thunder rolled across the sky, and hail mixed with fire beat down on the fields. Then locusts, carried in on the east wind, devoured every green thing the hail had spared. After that, for three days, a darkness so thick it could be felt covered the land.

Even in that darkness there was light in the places where the Israelites lived. Whenever a plague grew too hard to bear, Pharaoh gave in, again and again. But each time it stopped, he hardened his heart again. At last Moses announced the final plague. At midnight every firstborn in Egypt would die, from the firstborn son of Pharaoh on his throne to the firstborn son of the slave girl at her millstone, down to the firstborn of the livestock. A heavy silence settled over the land.

words.text: Let my people go, so that they may worship me in the wilderness.
This time I will send all my plagues on you, your officials and your people, so that you will know there is no one like me in all the earth.
This is the finger of God.

events.note: The plagues are sometimes read as judgments on the gods Egypt worshipped, such as the Nile and the sun. The Lord himself said he would bring judgment on all the gods of Egypt. Some try to explain the plagues as a chain of natural events, but views differ.
events.reflect: Pharaoh's heart did not harden all at once but a little more each time a plague stopped; whenever I get room to breathe, what am I putting off as my heart hardens?

quiz.q: Which plague could the Egyptian magicians not copy, leading them to say it was the finger of God?
quiz.explain: When Aaron struck the dust of the ground with his staff, it became gnats. The magicians could not produce gnats and said, This is the finger of God (Ex 8:16–19).

events.title: The First Passover
events.subtitle: Blood on the doorposts, a night passed over
story: The Lord said to Moses and Aaron, this month shall be for you the first month of the year. As the Lord had said, every household set aside a year-old lamb without blemish. On the fourteenth day of that month, at dusk, every household slaughtered its lamb. They dipped a bunch of hyssop in the blood in the basin and daubed it on the two doorposts and the lintel above. The red marks soaked into the evening light.

When night came, they ate the meat roasted over the fire, with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. They ate in haste, belts fastened, sandals on their feet, staffs in their hands. At midnight the Lord struck down the firstborn in the land of Egypt. A wail went up across all Egypt. From the firstborn son of Pharaoh on his throne to the firstborn of the prisoner in the dungeon, there was not a house without its dead. But the doors marked with blood the Lord passed over.

That very night Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron. Get up and leave my people. Go and serve the Lord, as you have asked. The people wrapped their dough, still unrisen, bowls and all, in their cloaks, hoisted it onto their shoulders and set out from Rameses. The men on foot alone numbered about six hundred thousand. It was the night that marked four hundred and thirty years since they had come to live in Egypt.

words.text: The blood will be a sign on the houses where you live. When I see the blood, I will pass over you. No plague will touch you when I strike Egypt.
Eat it in haste, with your belt fastened, your sandals on your feet and your staff in your hand. This is the Lord's Passover.
Get up and leave my people, you and the Israelites. Go and worship the Lord as you said. And ask a blessing for me too.

events.note: The Hebrew word for Passover, Pesach, is linked to the idea of passing over. Israel still remembers this night every year. The last meal Jesus shared with his disciples was also a meal at Passover time.
events.reflect: If what kept Israel safe that night was not their goodness but the blood on the doorposts, am I still looking for the grounds of my salvation in my own goodness?

quiz.q: According to Exodus 12, how long did the Israelites live in Egypt?
quiz.explain: At the end of four hundred and thirty years, on that very day, all the Lord's hosts went out of the land of Egypt (Ex 12:40–41).

img.credit: James Tissot, The Signs on the Door, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: Pillar of Cloud and Fire
events.subtitle: Not the short road, but the wilderness
story: The long column that had streamed out of Rameses reached Succoth. The road along the coast into the land of the Philistines was the shortest way. But God did not lead them by that road. He was concerned that if the people met with war, they would change their minds and go back to Egypt. So the column turned and went the long way, by the wilderness road toward the Red Sea.

Moses took the bones of Joseph with him as they set out. Joseph had left these words. God will surely come to you, and when he does, you must carry my bones up from here. It was the request Joseph had made the children of Israel swear to, centuries before. The multitude left Succoth and camped at Etham, at the edge of the wilderness. By day a pillar of cloud went ahead of them to lead the way, and by night a pillar of fire lit up the desert darkness.

Day and night the pillar never left its place before the people. Then the Lord said to Moses, Turn back and camp by the sea before Pi Hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea. It was a shore with nowhere left to retreat. The Lord went on. Pharaoh will think they are trapped and wandering in the wilderness, and he will pursue them. Then I will show my glory through Pharaoh and all his army.

words.text: If these people see war, they may change their minds and go back to Egypt.
I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and he will pursue you. Through Pharaoh and his army I will show my glory, and the Egyptians will know that I am the Lord.
God will surely come to help you. When he does, carry my bones up from this place.

events.note: The Way of the Philistines was the great road along the Mediterranean coast to Canaan, guarded by Egyptian fortresses. Succoth is thought to be Tell el Maskhuta, but the sites of Etham, Migdol and Pi Hahiroth are still uncertain.
events.reflect: If God led them by the wilderness road rather than the short way because he knew how weak they were, can I receive my own long way round as care rather than punishment?

quiz.q: What did Moses take with him out of Egypt?
quiz.explain: Moses took the bones of Joseph with him, because Joseph had made the Israelites swear to carry his bones up from Egypt (Ex 13:19; Gen 50:25).

img.title: The Israelites Leaving Egypt
img.credit: David Roberts, The Israelites Leaving Egypt, 1829 · Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery · Public domain

events.title: The Sea Divides
events.subtitle: Dry ground in the middle of the sea
story: No sooner had they let Israel go than Pharaoh and his officials regretted it. What have we done? We have let our slaves go free. Pharaoh took six hundred of his finest chariots and all the other chariots of Egypt and gave chase. Israel, camped by the sea, looked up, and out of a cloud of dust came the sound of hooves drawing near. The sea lay ahead, and an army behind.

The people wailed at Moses. Were there no graves in Egypt, that you brought us out to die in this wilderness? Moses cried out. Do not be afraid. Stand firm, and see how the Lord will save you today. The Lord will fight for you. That night the pillar of cloud that had gone before them moved round behind the camp. Toward Egypt it was darkness, and toward Israel it lit up the night.

Moses stretched out his hand over the sea. All night long the Lord drove the sea back with a strong east wind, and the waters parted and the seabed turned dry. The Israelites walked across on dry ground, with the waters standing like walls on their right and on their left. Toward dawn the wheels of the pursuing chariots came off, and the chariots lurched and swerved. Moses stretched out his hand again, and the sea returned to its place and covered the Egyptian army. When the people saw that great work, they feared the Lord, and they believed in the Lord and in his servant Moses.

words.text: Why are you crying out to me? Tell the Israelites to move forward. Raise your staff, stretch out your hand over the sea and divide it.
Do not be afraid. Stand still and see the salvation the Lord will bring you today. The Lord will fight for you; you need only be still.
Let us get away from Israel. The Lord is fighting for them against us.

events.note: In Hebrew, Yam Suph means sea of reeds. Where the crossing took place is debated. Suggestions include the lakes of the Isthmus of Suez, such as Lake Ballah, Lake Timsah and the Bitter Lakes, as well as the Gulf of Suez and the Gulf of Aqaba.
events.reflect: If “Stand still and see” and “Move forward” belong to the same scene, which faith do I need today: the faith that stops and waits, or the faith that takes one step onto the wet seabed?

quiz.q: How did God drive the sea back all night?
quiz.explain: When Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, the Lord drove the sea back all night with a strong east wind and turned it into dry land (Ex 14:21).

img.title: The Waters Are Divided
img.credit: James Tissot, The Waters Are Divided, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: The Song by the Sea
events.subtitle: The first praise, over the beat of tambourines
story: Morning broke over the shore. The wind that had raged all night had died away. Broken pieces of chariots washed up along the calm water's edge, and the people stood silent on the wet sand, gazing out to sea. Then Moses and the Israelites lifted their voices and began to sing. I will sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously. Horse and rider he has hurled into the sea.

The Lord is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation. He is my God, and I will exalt him. At the blast of the Lord's nostrils the waters piled up, the waves stood up like a wall, the deep waters congealed in the heart of the sea. Now the song looked ahead. Philistia and Edom, Moab and Canaan will tremble. The Lord will bring this people in and plant them on his holy mountain.

Then Miriam the prophet, Aaron's sister, took a tambourine in her hand. All the women followed her with tambourines, dancing. Above the sound of the tambourines on the sea breeze, Miriam's voice rang out to lead the song, and the women's voices answered after her. Sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously. Horse and rider he has hurled into the sea.

words.text: The Lord is my strength and my song; he is the one who saved me. He is my God, and I will praise him; my father's God, and I will lift him high.
Lord, who among the gods is like you? Who shines in holiness, awesome in praise, doing wonders?
Sing to the Lord, for he has won a great victory. Horse and rider he has thrown into the sea.

events.note: Because of its many archaic Hebrew expressions, this Song of the Sea is considered one of the oldest poems in the Bible. Miriam is the first woman in the Bible called a prophet, and the book of Revelation also pictures people singing the song of Moses.
events.reflect: As the song by the sea went beyond the enemy's fall to praise the Lord as my strength and my song, does my gratitude stop at what happened, or does it reach the one who did it?

quiz.q: What did the prophet Miriam hold in her hand as she sang with the women?
quiz.explain: Miriam the prophet, Aaron's sister, took a tambourine, and all the women followed her with tambourines and dancing (Ex 15:20).

img.title: The Songs of Joy
img.credit: James Tissot, The Songs of Joy, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: Bitter Water Made Sweet
events.subtitle: The first thirst, where the singing stopped
story: When the song by the sea had faded, Moses led the people away from the Red Sea into the Wilderness of Shur. For three days they walked and found no water. The sand underfoot burned hot, their lips cracked, and every step grew heavier. Wherever they looked there was only rock and sand, and even the wind carried the smell of dryness.

At last they came to Marah and found water. But it was too bitter to drink. The people grumbled against Moses. What are we supposed to drink? When Moses cried out to the Lord, the Lord showed him a piece of wood. He threw it into the water, and the bitter water turned sweet.

There the Lord gave the people a statute and a rule, and as he put them to the test, he said. If you listen to my voice and do what is right in my eyes, I will bring on you none of the diseases I brought on Egypt. I am the Lord who heals you. Then they came to Elim. Twelve springs were there and seventy palm trees, and by the water they pitched their tents.

words.text: If you listen carefully to the voice of the Lord your God and do what is right in my eyes, I will not bring on you any of the diseases I brought on Egypt. I am the Lord who heals you.
What are we supposed to drink?

events.note: Marah means bitter in Hebrew. Some identify Marah with Ain Hawara on the eastern shore of the Gulf of Suez and Elim with Wadi Gharandel, but the exact locations of both are unknown and views differ.
events.reflect: If what made the bitter water sweet was not the water but the wood thrown into it, what am I throwing into the bitter places of my life: complaint, or a cry to God?

quiz.q: What was at Elim, the place they reached after Marah?
options: Twelve springs and seventy palm trees
Seven springs and twelve palm trees
One well and forty fig trees
Three springs and seventy olive trees
quiz.explain: At Elim there were twelve springs and seventy palm trees, and the people camped there by the water (Ex 15:27).

img.title: Moses Sweetening the Bitter Waters of Marah
img.credit: Nicolas Poussin, Moses Sweetening the Bitter Waters of Marah, c. 1629–1630 · Baltimore Museum of Art · Public domain

events.title: Manna from Heaven
events.subtitle: Each morning, a day's bread on the dew
story: Leaving Elim, the people entered the Wilderness of Sin, between Elim and Sinai. It was the fifteenth day of the second month since they had come out of Egypt. When their food ran out, the whole community gathered around Moses and Aaron and grumbled. If only we had died by the Lord's hand in Egypt, when we sat beside the pots of meat and ate all the bread we wanted. You have brought us out into this wilderness to starve us all to death.

That evening quail flew in and covered the camp. The next morning, when the dew around the camp had lifted, something fine and white like frost lay over the wilderness. The people looked at one another and asked, What is it? Moses said, It is the bread the Lord has given you to eat. It tasted like wafers made with honey.

They were told to gather an omer for each person, just enough for that day. Some did not listen and kept a little until morning, and it bred worms and began to stink. On the sixth day they gathered twice as much, and on the seventh day, the Sabbath, they rested. The children of Israel ate this manna for forty years, until they came to a land where people lived, the border of Canaan.

words.text: Look, I will rain down bread from heaven for you. Each day the people are to go out and gather just enough for that day.
At twilight you will eat meat, and in the morning you will be filled with bread. Then you will know that I am the Lord your God.
This is the bread the Lord has given you to eat.

events.note: The name manna is explained as coming from the Hebrew man hu, meaning what is it. An omer was a tenth of an ephah, thought to be a little over two litres. Aaron put an omer of manna in a jar and placed it before the tablets of the covenant.
events.reflect: Manna could not be stored, so it made them look to heaven every day; are the things I store up for tomorrow robbing me of my reason to look to God today?

quiz.q: For how many years did the Israelites eat manna?
quiz.explain: The Israelites ate manna for forty years, until they came to a land where people lived, the border of Canaan (Ex 16:35).

img.title: The Gathering of the Manna
img.credit: James Tissot, The Gathering of the Manna, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: Water from the Rock
events.subtitle: Is the Lord among us or not?
story: Leaving the Wilderness of Sin, the people passed from place to place and camped at Rephidim. There was no water to drink there either. The sun beat down on the rocky valley, and the cries of thirsty children and animals filled the camp. The people crowded around Moses and quarrelled with him. Give us water to drink. Why did you bring us up out of Egypt, to make us and our children and our livestock die of thirst?

Moses cried out to the Lord. What am I to do with this people? A little more and they will stone me. The Lord said, Take some of the elders of Israel with you, and in your hand take the staff with which you struck the Nile, and walk on ahead of the people. I will stand before you there on the rock at Horeb. Strike the rock, and water will come out of it for the people to drink.

As the elders watched, holding their breath, Moses brought his staff down on the rock. Water gushed from the split rock and flowed. Moses called the place Massah, which means testing, and Meribah, which means quarrelling. For the people had quarrelled, and they had tested the Lord, saying, Is the Lord among us or not?

words.text: Look, I will stand before you there on the rock at Horeb. Strike the rock, and water will burst out of it for the people to drink.
Why do you quarrel with me? Why do you put the Lord to the test?
What am I to do with these people? A little more and they will stone me.

events.note: Rephidim is thought to be near Wadi Feiran in the southern Sinai Peninsula, but this is uncertain. Massah means testing and Meribah means quarrelling, and Psalm 95 recalls this event as an example of a hardened heart.
events.reflect: Even on the day they quarrelled over whether the Lord was among them, God was already standing on that rock; in the middle of my thirst, do I believe he got there before me?

quiz.q: What names did Moses give the place where water came from the rock?
quiz.explain: Because the people quarrelled and tested the Lord, Moses called the place Massah and Meribah (Ex 17:7).

img.title: Moses Strikes the Rock
img.credit: James Tissot, Moses Strikes the Rock, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: Two Raised Hands
events.subtitle: Hands that did not come down until sunset
story: At Rephidim, Amalek came and attacked Israel. Moses said to Joshua, Choose some men and go out to fight Amalek. Tomorrow I will stand on the top of the hill with the staff of God in my hand. The next day Joshua went out to fight, and Moses, Aaron and Hur went up to the top of the hill. From the valley below rose the clash of swords.

Whenever Moses held up his hands, Israel prevailed, and whenever he lowered them, Amalek prevailed. As the battle wore on, Moses' arms grew heavy. Aaron and Hur brought a stone and sat him on it, and they held up his hands, one on one side and one on the other. His hands stayed steady until the sun went down.

Joshua defeated Amalek and his people with the edge of the sword. The Lord said to Moses, Write this in a book to be remembered, and make sure Joshua hears it. I will blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven. Moses built an altar there and called it The Lord Is My Banner.

words.text: Write this in a book as a reminder, and make sure Joshua hears it. I will completely blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven.
Choose some men and go out to fight Amalek. Tomorrow I will stand on the top of the hill with the staff of God in my hand.

events.note: This is the first appearance of Joshua in the Bible. The Amalekites were descendants of Esau, nomads who roamed the Negev in the south and the Sinai wilderness. Deuteronomy says they attacked from behind those who were weary and lagging.
events.reflect: In the battle before me, which do I trust more, the hand that grips the sword or the hand raised to heaven, and when that hand sinks, do I know how to let the person beside me hold up my tired arms?

quiz.q: When Moses' arms grew tired, which two men held up his hands, one on each side?
quiz.explain: Aaron and Hur brought a stone for Moses to sit on and held up his hands, one on one side and one on the other (Ex 17:12).

img.credit: James Tissot, Moses on the Mountain During the Battle, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: Jethro's Advice
events.subtitle: An old priest's wisdom: do not carry it alone
story: News of all that God had done for Moses and for Israel reached Midian. Jethro, the priest of Midian, brought Moses' wife Zipporah and her two sons, Gershom and Eliezer, to the wilderness camp at the foot of the mountain of God, to see his son-in-law. Moses went out, bowed down to his father-in-law and kissed him. In the tent Moses told him everything, all that the Lord had done to Pharaoh and to Egypt, every hardship on the road, and how the Lord had saved them.

As he listened, Jethro's face brightened. He cried out. Praise the Lord, who has rescued you from the hand of the Egyptians and of Pharaoh. Now I know that the Lord is greater than all gods. Jethro brought a burnt offering and sacrifices to God. Aaron came, with all the elders of Israel, and they ate bread with him in the presence of God.

The next day Moses sat alone from morning till evening, hearing the people's disputes. When Jethro saw it, he said, Go on like this and you will wear yourself out, and the people with you. Appoint men you can trust, let them handle the small matters, and bring only the great ones to you. Moses did just as his father-in-law said. Then Jethro went home to his own land.

words.text: What you are doing is not good. You and the people with you will only wear yourselves out. The work is too heavy for you to carry alone.
Look among the people for capable men who fear God, who are honest and hate bribes, and appoint them as leaders over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens.
Now I know that the Lord is greater than all other gods.

events.note: The text says Jethro came to where Moses was camped at the mountain of God. So views differ on whether this happened at Rephidim or after they reached Sinai. The Midianites are thought to have lived in northwestern Arabia, east of the Gulf of Aqaba.
events.reflect: What Jethro corrected was not Moses' laziness but his excessive zeal; could my diligence be taking away the places where others ought to stand?

quiz.q: Which of these was not among the leaders Jethro advised Moses to appoint?
quiz.explain: Jethro advised appointing leaders of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens to judge the people (Ex 18:21). There were no leaders of five thousands.

img.credit: James Tissot, Jethro and Moses, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: God Comes Down on the Mountain
events.subtitle: A people carried on eagles' wings
story: Leaving Rephidim, the people entered the Wilderness of Sinai. It was in the third month after they had come out of Egypt. In a silent land where peaks of red granite pierced the sky, they camped before the mountain. Moses went up to God, and the Lord called to him from the mountain. Say this to the house of Jacob, and tell the children of Israel.

You have seen what I did to Egypt, and how I carried you on eagles' wings and brought you to myself. Now if you keep my covenant, you will be my treasured possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. When Moses passed on these words, the people answered with one voice. Everything the Lord has said, we will do. They washed their clothes, made themselves clean, and waited for the third day. A boundary was marked out all around the mountain.

On the morning of the third day there was thunder and lightning, a thick cloud covered the mountain, and a trumpet blast rang out loud. Everyone in the camp trembled. Moses led the people out, and they stood at the foot of the mountain. The Lord came down upon it in fire, and the mountain poured out smoke like a furnace and shook violently. The sound of the trumpet grew louder and louder.

words.text: You have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I carried you to myself as an eagle carries its young on its wings.
The whole earth is mine, but if you truly listen to me and keep my covenant, you will be for me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.
We will do everything the Lord has said.

events.note: Mount Sinai is traditionally identified with Jebel Musa, the Mountain of Moses, in the southern Sinai Peninsula, about 2,285 metres high. But other suggestions include Jebel Serbal, the northern part of the peninsula and mountains in northwestern Arabia, so the exact location is unknown.
events.reflect: Before giving the law, God first said he had carried them on eagles' wings and brought them to himself; do I know my life with God as a list of things to do, or as the story of a love that carried me here?

quiz.q: At Sinai, what did God say Israel would become if they kept the covenant?
options: A kingdom of priests and a holy nation
quiz.explain: If they kept the covenant, Israel would be God's treasured possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation (Ex 19:5–6).

img.title: Moses on Mount Sinai
img.credit: Jean-Léon Gérôme, Moses on Mount Sinai, c. 1895–1900 · Private collection · Public domain

events.title: The Ten Words
events.subtitle: Words from the one who set them free
story: Smoke wrapped the whole mountain, and flames flickered at its summit. From within it God himself began to speak, and the whole people at the foot of the mountain held their breath and heard his voice. The first words were not a command. I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. On that rescue, now, the ten words began to be laid down one by one.

You shall have no other gods besides me. Do not make a carved image and bow down before it. Do not take the name of the Lord your God lightly. Six days you shall work, but remember the seventh day, the Sabbath, and keep it holy. Honour your father and your mother. Do not murder, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not bear false witness against your neighbour, do not covet your neighbour's house or anything that is his.

As the thunder rolled and the lightning flashed and the trumpet sounded long, and the mountain poured out smoke, the people trembled, drew back and stood far off. They clung to Moses. You speak to us, and we will listen. If God speaks to us himself, we feel we will die. Moses answered, Do not be afraid. God has come to test you, and to keep you from sinning. The people stood far off, while Moses alone drew near to the thick darkness where God was.

words.text: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. You shall have no other gods before me.
Honour your father and your mother, so that you may live long in the land the Lord your God is giving you.
You speak to us, and we will listen. If God speaks to us directly, we feel we will die.
Do not be afraid. God has come to test you, so that the fear of him will keep you from sinning.

events.note: Exodus 34 and Deuteronomy 4 call these the ten words. The way they are divided into ten differs slightly between the Jewish, Catholic and Lutheran, and Reformed traditions. The same words appear again in Deuteronomy 5.
events.reflect: If the ten words begin with the Lord who brought you out of the house of slavery, are the commandments a chain that binds me again, or a fence of freedom that keeps me from going back into slavery?

quiz.q: Which of the ten words comes with the promise that you may live long in the land?
quiz.explain: Honouring your parents came with the promise of a long life in the land the Lord was giving (Ex 20:12).

img.title: Moses and the Ten Commandments
img.credit: James Tissot, Moses and the Ten Commandments, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: The Blood of the Covenant
events.subtitle: A covenant sealed in blood and shared at a meal
story: Moses told the people all the words the Lord had spoken. The people cried out with one voice. All the words the Lord has spoken, we will do. Moses wrote down every one of those words. Early the next morning he built an altar at the foot of the mountain and set up twelve stone pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel. Young men offered burnt offerings and sacrificed bulls as peace offerings, and smoke rose above the altar.

Moses poured half of the blood into basins, and the other half he splashed against the altar. Then he opened the book of the covenant and read it aloud for the people to hear. When he had finished, the people answered again. All that the Lord has spoken we will do, and we will obey. Moses took the blood from the basins and sprinkled it on the people. See, this is the blood of the covenant the Lord has made with you, in keeping with all these words.

Moses and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel went up the mountain. When they saw the God of Israel, beneath his feet was something like a pavement of sapphire, clear as the sky itself. God did not lay a hand on them, and they beheld God, and they ate and drank. Some time later the cloud covered the mountain for six days, and on the seventh day the Lord called to Moses from within the cloud. Moses went into the glory that blazed like a consuming fire, and he stayed on the mountain forty days and forty nights.

words.text: Come up to me on the mountain and wait there. I will give you the tablets of stone, with the law and commands I have written to teach the people.
Look, this is the blood of the covenant the Lord has made with you in keeping with all these words.
We will do everything the Lord has said, and we will obey.

events.note: In the ancient Near East, covenants were often made with a ceremony of slaughtering animals and eating together. The blood sprinkled at the making of the Sinai covenant points ahead to the blood of the covenant that Jesus spoke of when he lifted the cup at the Last Supper.
events.reflect: If the blood of the covenant was sprinkled over the people's vow to do everything, on the day my resolve collapses, do I lean on my own promise, or on his promise sealed in blood?

quiz.q: How many stone pillars did Moses set up beside the altar, one for each tribe of Israel?
quiz.explain: Moses built an altar at the foot of the mountain and set up twelve stone pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel (Ex 24:4).

img.title: Moses Forbids the People to Follow Him
img.credit: James Tissot, Moses Forbids the People to Follow Him, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: The Golden Calf
events.subtitle: A god shaped by hands that could not bear to wait
story: Days went by, and still Moses did not come down from the mountain. The people, staring up at the cloud-covered summit, grew more and more uneasy. They crowded around Aaron. We do not know what has become of this man who brought us out of Egypt. Make us a god to go before us. Aaron collected their gold earrings, melted them down, shaped the gold with a carving tool and made a calf.

The people cried out. Israel, this is your god, who brought you out of Egypt. The next morning a feast was held before the altar. The people ate and drank, and got up to dance. At that very hour, on the mountain, the Lord in his anger said to Moses. Go down at once, your people have become corrupt. I will wipe them out. Moses fell down and pleaded. Remember the promise you made to Abraham, to Isaac and to Israel. And the Lord turned back from the disaster he had meant to bring.

Moses came down the mountain, holding the two stone tablets God himself had engraved. As he neared the camp he heard singing, and he saw the crowd circling the golden calf. Moses flung the tablets down and shattered them at the foot of the mountain. He burned the calf, ground it to powder, scattered it on the water and made the people drink it. Then he went back up the mountain and spoke to the Lord. Forgive the sin of this people. And if you will not, then blot my name out of your book.

words.text: Go down at once. Your people, whom you brought out of Egypt, have become corrupt. They have turned so quickly from the way I commanded, casting a calf and bowing down to it.
These people have committed a great sin. Now please forgive their sin. But if not, then blot my name out of the book you have written.
They gave me the gold, and I threw it into the fire, and out came this calf.

events.note: The golden calf is thought to be connected with Apis, the bull god of Egypt, or with the bull statues of Canaan seen as pedestals on which a god stood, and views differ. Later the same words are repeated before the golden calves Jeroboam set up at Bethel and Dan.
events.reflect: Like Aaron's excuse, “I threw the gold into the fire and out came this calf,” am I passing off an idol I shaped with my own hands as something that simply happened?

quiz.q: What did Moses do with the golden calf the people made?
options: Burned it, ground it to powder, scattered it on water and made them drink it
Threw it into the Red Sea
quiz.explain: Moses burned the calf in the fire, ground it to powder, scattered it on the water and made the Israelites drink it (Ex 32:20).

img.title: The Golden Calf
img.credit: James Tissot, The Golden Calf, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: The Glory Passes By
events.subtitle: The name heard from a cleft in the rock
story: The wound left by the golden calf was still raw in the camp. Moses pleaded with the Lord once more. Remember that this nation is your people. If you yourself do not go with us, do not send us up from here. Even after the Lord answered that he himself would go, Moses pressed one step further. Show me your glory.

The Lord answered. I will make all my goodness pass before you. But you cannot see my face, for no one may see me and live. Stand here on the rock beside me. When my glory passes by, I will put you in a cleft of the rock and cover you with my hand until I have passed. At first light the next morning, Moses cut two stone tablets like the first ones and climbed Mount Sinai alone.

The Lord came down in the cloud and stood there with him, and passed in front of him, proclaiming. The Lord, the Lord, a God compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness. Moses quickly bowed to the ground and worshipped. Lord, go with us. Forgive our sin and take us as your own. The Lord answered, See, I am making a covenant.

words.text: The Lord, the Lord, a God compassionate and gracious, slow to anger and overflowing with steadfast love and faithfulness. He shows love to a thousand generations and forgives wrongdoing and sin.
My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest.
Show me your glory.

events.note: This confession in Exodus 34:6–7 is the self-description of God most often echoed in the Old Testament. It is repeated in almost the same words in many places, including Numbers 14, Psalm 103 and Jonah 4.
events.reflect: When Moses asked to see his glory, God let him hear his name of compassion; while I ask God for wonders, do I actually want to know who he is?

quiz.q: Where did God put Moses as his glory passed by?
options: At the entrance of the tent of meeting
In a cleft of the rock
At the altar below the mountain
quiz.explain: The Lord said that as his glory passed by, he would put Moses in a cleft of the rock and cover him with his hand (Ex 33:22).

img.title: Moses with the Tablets of the Law
img.credit: Rembrandt, Moses with the Tablets of the Law, 1659 · Gemäldegalerie, Berlin · Public domain

events.title: Glory Fills the Tabernacle
events.subtitle: God's house set up in the middle of the wilderness
story: In the middle of the tent village below Mount Sinai, Moses began to set up the tabernacle. It was the first day of the first month, in the second year after they had left Egypt. One by one the silver bases were laid on the sand, and on them the gold-covered frames rose upright. He fitted the crossbars, raised the posts and spread the coverings over the top, and there in the middle of the windblown camp the house of God took shape.

Moses placed the tablets of the testimony in the ark, slid the poles into place and covered it with the atonement cover. He brought the ark into the tabernacle and hung the curtain to screen it. He set the table for the bread, the lampstand and the gold altar of incense in their places, and in the courtyard the altar of burnt offering and the basin. Down to raising the hangings around the courtyard and hanging the curtain at its gate, he finished everything just as the Lord had commanded.

Then the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the Lord filled the tabernacle. Not even Moses could go inside. From that day on, whenever the cloud lifted from the tabernacle, the people packed up and set out, and whenever the cloud stayed, they stayed where they were. By day the cloud rested over the tabernacle, and by night fire burned within it, and all Israel saw it, every step of the way.

words.text: On the first day of the first month, set up the tabernacle, the tent of meeting.
Dress Aaron in the sacred garments, anoint him and set him apart, so that he may serve me as priest.

events.note: The tabernacle was set up on the first day of the first month of the second year after the exodus, almost a year after leaving Egypt. Its courtyard was a hundred cubits long and fifty cubits wide, roughly 45 by 22 metres.
events.reflect: If the tent so full of glory that even Moses could not enter later came to us as the Word who pitched his tent among us, how lightly am I treating that presence?

quiz.q: When the cloud covered the tent of meeting and the glory of the Lord filled the tabernacle, what happened to Moses?
options: He could not enter the tent of meeting
quiz.explain: Because the cloud settled on the tent of meeting and the glory of the Lord filled the tabernacle, Moses could not enter the tent of meeting (Ex 40:35).

img.credit: James Tissot, Bezalel, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: Graves of Craving
events.subtitle: Mouths that demanded meat became graves
story: Not long after they left Mount Sinai, the sound of complaining rose from the edge of the camp. Fire from the Lord blazed up at the outskirts, and the people cried out to Moses. Moses prayed, and the fire died down. They named the place where the fire had burned Taberah. But among the mixed crowd living with Israel, craving began to spread once more. The Israelites too wept again and said.

Who will give us meat to eat? We remember the fish we ate in Egypt for nothing, the cucumbers and the melons, the leeks, the onions and the garlic. Now there is nothing to look at but this manna, like coriander seed. From the door of every tent came the sound of weeping. Moses poured out his heart before the Lord as if he were falling apart. I cannot carry this whole people alone. The burden is too heavy for me. The Lord had him gather seventy elders at the tent of meeting, and he shared with them the spirit that was on Moses.

Then a wind went out from the Lord and drove flocks of quail in from the sea. The quail lay all around the camp, a day's walk in every direction, two cubits deep above the ground. All that day and all night and all the next day, the people gathered them without stopping. But while the meat was still between their teeth, the anger of the Lord came down, and a great plague struck the people. The place where those who had craved were buried was called Kibroth Hattaavah, the graves of craving.

words.text: Is my arm too short? Now you will see with your own eyes whether my word comes true or not.
I will come down and speak with you there. I will take some of the Spirit that is on you and give it to them, so that you will not carry the burden of the people alone.
Are you jealous for my sake? I wish all the Lord's people were prophets and that the Lord would put his Spirit on them all.

events.note: Kibroth Hattaavah means graves of craving. Its exact location is unknown, but it is thought to lie somewhere northeast of Mount Sinai. Quail are migratory birds that cross the Sinai Peninsula in spring and autumn, and flocks exhausted from crossing the sea often come down low near the ground.
events.reflect: Before craving was a longing for what they lacked, it was weariness with what they had been given; am I tired of the grace I receive each day, longing for the tables of Egypt?

quiz.q: Which of these was not among the Egyptian foods the people longed for?
quiz.explain: The people longed for the fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic they had eaten in Egypt (Num 11:5).

img.title: Moses Showing the Quails to the Israelites
img.credit: Andrea Schiavone, Moses Showing the Quails to the Israelites, c. 1545 · The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Public domain

events.title: The Twelve Spies
events.subtitle: They saw the same land and came back with different hearts
story: At the camp in the Wilderness of Paran, Moses called out twelve men, a leader from each tribe. To Hoshea son of Nun he gave a new name, Joshua. Moses told them, go up into the Negev, then on into the hill country. See whether the land is good, whether the people are strong or weak, and bring back some of its fruit. It was the season of the first ripe grapes, and the twelve went up past Hebron, as far as Rehob in the far north, exploring the land for forty days.

When they returned, two men were carrying between them, on a pole, a single cluster of grapes cut in the Valley of Eshcol. They brought pomegranates and figs as well. They reported. It truly is a land flowing with milk and honey. But the people there are strong, the cities are large and fortified, and we even saw the descendants of Anak. Caleb quieted the stirring crowd and called out. Let us go up at once and take the land, for we can certainly do it. But the others shook their heads. Beside them we were like grasshoppers.

That night the whole community wept aloud. If only we had died in Egypt. Let us choose a leader and go back to Egypt. Joshua and Caleb tore their clothes and cried out. The Lord is with us. Do not be afraid of them. But the whole community talked of stoning them. Just then the glory of the Lord appeared above the tent of meeting. The Lord said, How long will this people treat me with contempt? Moses fell down and pleaded. In your great steadfast love, forgive this people. The Lord forgave them, yet the generation that would not trust God would never see the promised land, and would wander in the wilderness for forty years. Only Caleb and Joshua, and the children of that generation, would go into the land.

words.text: My servant Caleb has a different spirit and has followed me wholeheartedly. I will bring him into the land he walked on, and his descendants will inherit it.
For the forty days you explored the land, a year for each day, you will bear the burden of your sins for forty years.
Let us go up right now and take the land. We can certainly overcome it.

events.note: Many identify Kadesh Barnea with the spring of Ain el Qudeirat south of the Negev, but there are other candidates nearby, such as Ain Qadeis, and views differ. Eshcol means cluster, and the valley is thought to be near Hebron.
events.reflect: What the ten men measured wrongly was not the giants' height but the size of God; while I measure my problems so precisely, how small am I measuring God?

quiz.q: What was the original name of the man Moses renamed Joshua?
quiz.explain: Moses gave Hoshea son of Nun the name Joshua (Num 13:16).

img.credit: James Tissot, The Grapes of Canaan, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: The Staff That Budded
events.subtitle: Almond blossoms on a dry stick
story: Korah, a Levite, together with Dathan and Abiram of the tribe of Reuben and two hundred and fifty well-known leaders, rose up to block the way of Moses and Aaron. They cried out, the whole community is holy, so why do you set yourselves above us? At that, Moses fell face down. Moses said. Tomorrow all of you, put fire and incense in your censers before the Lord, and you will see whom the Lord chooses. Moses summoned Dathan and Abiram, but they refused to come. Is it not enough that you brought us up out of Egypt, a land flowing with milk and honey, to kill us in the wilderness?

The moment Moses finished saying, this is how you will know that the Lord has sent me, the ground beneath them split apart. The earth opened its mouth, swallowed them and their households, and closed again. Then fire came out from the Lord and consumed the two hundred and fifty men holding censers. The next day the whole community grumbled again, and a plague began to spread. Aaron took his censer and ran into the midst of the assembly, and he stood between the dead and the living. And the plague stopped.

The Lord had them place twelve staffs, one for each tribe, before the ark of the testimony in the tent of meeting. On the staff of Levi was written Aaron's name. The Lord said to Moses. The staff of the man I choose will sprout. The next morning, when Moses went into the tent, Aaron's staff had sprouted, blossomed and borne ripe almonds. Dead wood had come to life in a single night.

words.text: The staff of the man I choose will sprout. In this way I will put an end to the grumbling of the Israelites against you.
Put Aaron's staff back in front of the ark of the covenant, as a sign to the rebellious.
This is how you will know that the Lord has sent me to do all these things, and that it was not my own idea.

events.note: In the land of Israel the almond tree is the first to blossom in late winter, which earned it a Hebrew name meaning the wakeful tree. The letter to the Hebrews says Aaron's budded staff was kept inside the ark of the covenant. The text does not say in which year of the wilderness journey this happened.
events.reflect: God did not argue with the rebels but made a dry staff blossom; where I long to be recognised, am I straining to prove myself, or waiting for the time he makes it bloom?

quiz.q: What fruit appeared on Aaron's staff overnight?
quiz.explain: Aaron's staff had sprouted, blossomed and produced almonds (Num 17:8).

img.credit: Sandro Botticelli, The Punishment of Korah, 1481–1482 · Sistine Chapel · Public domain

events.title: The Waters of Meribah
events.subtitle: A hand that struck the rock twice
story: At Kadesh in the Wilderness of Zin, the whole community of Israel unpacked their loads. It was the first month. There Miriam died and was buried. She was the sister of Moses and Aaron, the prophet who had taken up her tambourine and sung before the women on the day they crossed the sea. Her grave was dug in the wilderness earth. Before the grief had even passed, the camp ran out of water.

The people crowded around Moses and Aaron and quarrelled with them. If only we had died when our brothers died before the Lord. Why did you bring us to this terrible place? There is no grain here, no figs, no grapes, no pomegranates, and not even water to drink. When the two of them fell face down at the door of the tent of meeting, the glory of the Lord appeared. The Lord said, take the staff and gather the community. Before their eyes, speak to the rock and it will pour out its water.

Moses and Aaron gathered the assembly in front of the rock. Moses shouted at them. Listen, you rebels. Must we bring water for you out of this rock? Moses raised his hand and struck the rock twice with his staff. Water came pouring out, and the community and their animals drank. But the Lord said to the two of them, Because you did not trust me, and did not show my holiness, you will not lead this community into the land I have given them. The people called those waters Meribah.

words.text: Take the staff and gather the community. Speak to that rock as they watch, and it will pour out its water.
You did not trust me enough to show my holiness before the people. So you will not bring this community into the land I have given them.
Listen, you rebels. Must we bring water out of this rock for you?

events.note: Meribah means quarrelling. The text says only the first month, but since Aaron died in the fifth month of the fortieth year in the wilderness, this event is thought to belong to that year too. Early in the exodus, at Rephidim, water had also come from a rock, and that place too was called Meribah.
events.reflect: The same rock, the same staff, yet this time God said to speak to the rock; by clinging to what worked last time, am I missing the way God wants now?

quiz.q: What did the Lord tell Moses to do before the rock?
options: Strike the rock once with his staff
Build an altar before the rock
quiz.explain: The Lord told him to speak to the rock in front of the community, but Moses struck the rock twice with his staff (Num 20:8, 11).

img.credit: James Tissot, Moses Smites the Rock in the Desert, c. 1896–1902 · The Jewish Museum, New York · Public domain

events.title: Aaron on Mount Hor
events.subtitle: The high priest's robes pass to his son
story: The whole community of Israel left Kadesh and came to Mount Hor, on the border of the land of Edom. The red rock mountain caught the evening sun and glowed as if on fire. There the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron. Aaron will now be gathered to his people. Because you rebelled against my word at the waters of Meribah, he will not enter the land I have given Israel.

Moses took Aaron and his son Eleazar and climbed the mountain while the whole community watched. Behind the three men, climbing the stony slope, the shadows stretched long. On the summit Moses took the high priest's garments off his brother one by one and put them on Eleazar. They were the robes in which Aaron had stood before the altar for nearly forty years, bearing the sins of the people.

And there on the mountaintop Aaron died. Only two came down the mountain, Moses and Eleazar. When all Israel learned that Aaron was dead, they mourned for him thirty days. The wilderness wind swept through the camp, and in the midst of the weeping stood Eleazar, wearing the high priest's robes.

words.text: Aaron will now be gathered to his ancestors. Because you rebelled against my word at the waters of Meribah, he will not enter the land I have given the Israelites.
Remove Aaron's garments and put them on his son Eleazar. Aaron will die there and be gathered to his ancestors.

events.note: Numbers 33 says Aaron died on the first day of the fifth month of the fortieth year after the exodus, at the age of one hundred and twenty-three. Tradition identifies Mount Hor with Jebel Harun near Petra, where a shrine to Aaron's tomb stands, but others place it at a mountain nearer Kadesh, so the location is uncertain.
events.reflect: Aaron never set foot in the promised land, yet his robes passed on to the next generation; can I rejoice more that God's work goes on than that my name remains?

quiz.q: Who put on Aaron's priestly garments on Mount Hor?
quiz.explain: Moses took off Aaron's garments and put them on his son Eleazar, and Aaron died on the mountaintop (Num 20:28).

events.title: The Bronze Snake on a Pole
events.subtitle: Look and live
story: Leaving Mount Hor, Israel turned onto the Red Sea road to go around the land of Edom. With the promised land right before them, they were heading south again. The detour stretched on endlessly along the dry valleys. Hot winds whipped up the sand, and the longer the road, the more the people's hearts ran dry.

At last they poured it all out against God and against Moses. Why have you brought us up out of Egypt to die in this wilderness? There is no food and no water, and we are sick of this miserable food. Then the Lord sent fiery serpents among them. The snakes came into the camp and bit the people, and many fell and died. The people crowded to Moses and pleaded. We have sinned, for we spoke against the Lord and against you. Take these snakes away from us.

Moses prayed for the people, and the Lord said, Make a fiery serpent and set it on a pole. Anyone who is bitten and looks at it will live. Moses made a snake out of bronze and hung it high at the top of a pole, where it could be seen from anywhere in the camp. Even someone bitten and fallen, if he lifted his head and looked at the bronze snake, lived.

words.text: Make the shape of a venomous snake and fix it on a pole. Anyone who has been bitten by a snake will live if they look at it.
We sinned when we spoke against the Lord and against you. Pray to the Lord to take these snakes away from us.

events.note: The text does not say where the bronze snake was set up, but following the list of stages in Numbers 33 it is placed at Punon in the Arabah. Punon is thought to be Feinan in present-day Jordan, the site of ancient copper mines. Centuries later King Hezekiah broke the bronze snake in pieces because people were burning incense to it.
events.reflect: What saved the people was not the power of the bronze snake but eyes lifted up to look, and Jesus said he too must be lifted up in the same way; am I staring only at my own wounds, or lifting my head to look at him?

quiz.q: How could a person bitten by a venomous snake live?
options: By receiving Moses' laying on of hands
By offering a lamb on the altar
By looking at the bronze snake on the pole
By going outside the camp to wash
quiz.explain: Whenever someone bitten by a snake looked at the bronze snake, they lived (Num 21:9).

events.title: Winning the Land East of the Jordan
events.subtitle: A battle that began on the King's Highway
story: Having come up around the wilderness, Israel stood north of the Arnon Valley, before the land of Sihon king of the Amorites. Israel sent messengers to Sihon. Let us pass through your land. We will not go into any field or vineyard, nor drink water from any well. We will keep to the King's Highway until we are out of your land. But Sihon would not let them pass.

Sihon gathered all his people, marched out into the wilderness and met Israel at Jahaz. Israel struck him with the edge of the sword and took his land from the Arnon to the Jabbok River. Israel moved into Sihon's royal city of Heshbon and the villages around it. It was the very city the old singers had sung of, the city from which fire went out and consumed Moab.

Israel turned again and went up toward Bashan. Og king of Bashan came out with his whole army to meet them at Edrei. The Lord said to Moses, Do not be afraid of him, for I have handed him over to you, with his people and his land. Israel struck down Og, his sons and all his people and took possession of his land. For the first time, the high plains east of the Jordan became the land of Israel.

words.text: Do not be afraid of him. I have handed him over to you, with his people and his land. Do to him as you did to Sihon king of the Amorites, who ruled in Heshbon.
Let us pass through your land. We will not go into any field or vineyard or drink water from any well. We will keep to the King's Highway.

events.note: Heshbon is identified with Tell Hesban, north of Madaba in Jordan, but excavations have found no clear remains of a town from this period, so views differ. The southern border, the Arnon, is today's Wadi Mujib, and the northern border, the Jabbok, is the Zarqa River.
events.reflect: When their request to pass along the King's Highway was refused, God turned that blocked road into their first inheritance; standing before a closed door, do I have eyes to see what has been prepared beyond it?

quiz.q: Og, whom Israel defeated at Edrei, was king of which land?
quiz.explain: Og king of Bashan came out to fight at Edrei, and Israel struck him down and took his land (Num 21:33, 35).

events.title: Balaam and the Donkey
events.subtitle: Blessing pours from a mouth that came to curse
story: Israel camped on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho. Looking down on that great multitude, Balak king of Moab trembled with fear. He sent for Balaam son of Beor, at Pethor by the Euphrates. Envoys came with the fee for divination in their hands and delivered Balak's message. Come and curse this people for me. I know that whoever you bless is blessed, and whoever you curse is cursed.

At first the Lord told Balaam not to go, but when envoys of higher rank came again, the Lord let him go, as long as he said only what he was told. Balaam rose early in the morning, saddled his donkey and set out. But suddenly the donkey turned off the road into a field. Between the vineyard walls she pressed against the wall and crushed her master's foot, and on a narrower path still she simply lay down. Each time, Balaam flew into a rage and beat her. Only the donkey could see the angel of the Lord standing in the road with a drawn sword. Then the Lord opened the donkey's mouth, and she spoke. What have I done to you, that you have beaten me three times? Only then were Balaam's eyes opened, and seeing the angel, he fell face down.

Balak took Balaam up to high places, built seven altars and offered a bull and a ram on each. But every time Balaam opened his mouth, blessing poured out instead of curse. How beautiful are your tents, Jacob, how fair your dwellings, Israel. A star will come out of Jacob, and a sceptre will rise from Israel. Balak struck his hands together in fury, but Balaam got up and went back to his own home.

words.text: Do not go with them. You must not curse that people, for they are blessed.
Since these men have come to summon you, get up and go with them. But say only what I tell you.
I see him, but not now; I look at him, but not near. A star will come out of Jacob, and a scepter will rise out of Israel.

events.note: A plaster inscription found in 1967 at Deir Alla in the Jordan Valley mentions a seer named Balaam son of Beor. Written around the eighth century BC, it shows that Balaam was long remembered east of the Jordan. Pethor is thought to have been near the upper Euphrates.
events.reflect: The donkey saw the angel blocking the road while the famous seer did not; so absorbed in my own plans, am I treating the stop signs God puts up as nothing but annoying interruptions?

quiz.q: Why did Balaam's donkey turn off the road and finally lie down?
options: The angel of the Lord with a sword was blocking the road
There was a snake on the road
quiz.explain: The donkey saw the angel of the Lord standing in the road with a drawn sword, and turned off the road (Num 22:23).

events.title: Hear, O Israel
events.subtitle: Words to engrave on the heart and write on the doorposts
story: In the land of Moab, east of the Jordan, the forty years in the wilderness were almost over. Across the river, where Moses raised his hand to point, the palm groves of Jericho could be glimpsed in the distance. The new generation, born and raised in the wilderness, gathered one by one and sat down before their aged leader. Moses looked around at them and began to speak. When you enter that land, there are words you must keep. With the last of his strength he gave them those words.

Hear, O Israel. The Lord our God is one. Love him with all your heart, with all your soul and with all your strength. Engrave on your heart these words I speak to you today. Tell them to your children again and again, when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up. Tie them on your wrist as a sign and bind them on your forehead, and write them on the doorposts of your house and on your gates.

Then Moses' voice grew stern. When you have great and fine cities you did not build, houses full of good things you did not fill, wells you did not dig, vineyards and olive groves you did not plant, and you eat your fill, be careful. Do not forget the Lord who brought you out of the house of slavery. And one day, when your children ask what these words mean, answer them like this. We were Pharaoh's slaves in Egypt, and the Lord brought us out of there with a mighty hand.

words.text: Hear, O Israel. The Lord our God, the Lord is one. Love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul and with all your strength.
Keep these words I give you today in your heart. Repeat them to your children, and talk about them when you are at home and when you are on the road, when you lie down and when you get up.
Then be careful. Do not forget the Lord who brought you out of Egypt, the land of slavery.

events.note: The Hebrew word Shema, meaning hear, became the name of this confession. Jews still recite these words morning and evening and fix small cases containing scripture to their doorposts. Jesus named Deuteronomy 6:5 the greatest commandment, and he quoted this chapter during his testing in the wilderness.
events.reflect: The words that begin with “Hear” pass through “Love” and go on to “Do not forget”; on full and comfortable days, does my faith still remember why I love God?

quiz.q: When children ask the meaning of these laws, what were the parents to tell them first?
options: We received the law at Sinai
We were Pharaoh's slaves in Egypt
We walked forty years in the wilderness
quiz.explain: When your children ask, answer that we were Pharaoh's slaves in Egypt, but the Lord brought us out with a mighty hand (Deut 6:20–21).

events.title: The Land Seen from Mount Nebo
events.subtitle: A river he did not cross, a land he gazed on to the end
story: Leaving the people on the plains of Moab, Moses climbed Mount Nebo alone. As he made his way up the steep path, the sounds of the camp grew fainter and fainter. When he reached the top of Pisgah, facing Jericho, the wind swept over the dry grass. He was a hundred and twenty years old. Yet his eyes were not dim, and his strength had not left him.

The Lord showed him the whole land. Gilead as far north as Dan, the land of Naphtali, of Ephraim and Manasseh, all the land of Judah reaching to the western sea. The Negev in the south, and the valley of Jericho, the city of palms, as far as Zoar. The Lord said, This is the land I swore to Abraham, to Isaac and to Jacob that I would give to their descendants. I have let you see it with your own eyes, but you will not cross over into it.

There in the land of Moab, Moses the servant of the Lord died, as the Lord had said. The Lord himself buried him in the valley opposite Beth Peor, but to this day no one knows where his grave is. The children of Israel wept for Moses on the plains of Moab for thirty days. Joshua, on whom Moses had laid his hands, was filled with the spirit of wisdom, and the people listened to him. Never again has there risen a prophet like Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face.

words.text: This is the land I swore to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob that I would give to their descendants. I have let you see it with your own eyes, but you will not cross over into it.
Since then no prophet like Moses has risen in Israel, whom the Lord knew face to face.

events.note: Mount Nebo is thought to be a peak in Jordan a little over 700 metres high. On a clear day the Dead Sea, the oasis of Jericho and even the ridges toward Jerusalem can be seen from it. Pisgah is taken to be the name for the summit of that range.
events.reflect: If Moses, who could only look at the land from Mount Nebo, later stood in it with Jesus on the mountain of the transfiguration, can I entrust the promises I will not see fulfilled in my lifetime to God's longer time?

quiz.q: How old was Moses when he died?
quiz.explain: Moses was a hundred and twenty years old when he died, yet his eyes were not dim and his strength had not left him (Deut 34:7). A hundred and ten was Joshua's age when he died.

events.title: Be Strong and Courageous
events.subtitle: A voice heard again where Moses had been
story: The days of weeping for Moses came to an end. In the camp east of the Jordan, the tents lay quiet in the shade of the acacia trees. Then the Lord spoke to Joshua son of Nun, who had served at Moses' side. My servant Moses is dead. Now get up, you and all this people, cross the Jordan, and go into the land I am giving them.

Every place the sole of your foot treads I have given you. From the wilderness and Lebanon to the great river Euphrates, and to the great sea where the sun goes down, will be your land. As I was with Moses, so I will be with you. I will never leave you or forsake you. Do not let this book of the law depart from your mouth, and turn it over in your mind day and night. Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid.

Joshua gave orders to the officers of the people. Go through the camp and tell them, Get your provisions ready, for within three days we cross the Jordan. To the fighting men of Reuben, Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh, who had received land east of the Jordan, he said they must cross over armed, ahead of their brothers. They answered, Whatever you command us we will do, and wherever you send us we will go. Only be strong and courageous.

words.text: Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid or discouraged, for I, the Lord your God, am with you wherever you go.
As I was with Moses, so I will be with you. I will not leave you, and I will never abandon you.
Keep the words of this book of the law always on your lips and turn them over day and night. Then your way will open before you, and you will act wisely.
Whatever you command us we will do, and wherever you send us we will go. Only be strong and courageous.

events.note: The name Joshua means the Lord is salvation. Moses gave it to him in place of his original name, Hoshea. In Greek it becomes the same name as Jesus. Shittim means acacias, and its exact location remains a matter of conjecture.
events.reflect: God said “Be strong and courageous” again and again, likely because Joshua was that afraid; do I think I can obey only once my fear is gone, or do I hold on to the word and go forward while still afraid?

quiz.q: Within how many days did Joshua tell the people they would cross the Jordan?
quiz.explain: Joshua commanded, Get your provisions ready, for within three days you will cross this Jordan (Josh 1:11).
